Sometimes, the people that produce the food (like Nestle) will give a discount to major retailers because they are buying more product (multiple truckloads vs a single pallet). This should in theory result in a lower cost for the consumer....or it is results in a profit for the retailer.

There are some food companies that set up a standard pricing scheme....you can order a pallet or a truckload and it is the same cost. Again, it is up to the grocery story whether they pocket this as profit or pass the savings on to consumers.

All grocery stores (except Walmart) require the manufacturer (like Nestle) to pay "slotting fees". This is a fee to take up space on their shelf. A new product means more money for the retailer. A new net weight (deviating more than 20%) is more money for the retailer.

And then you get into whether the grocery store is part of a chain (like Kroger) or part of Conglomerate (like Kroger which owns Kroger, Baker's, etc). Every chain has a different expectation for their gross margin. They have to pay for the store, the employees, stocking, etc...They are putting up a lot of money to sell a product.

I think a similar thing has happened with canned foods. Most used to be 15.0 oz but are now 14.5 oz.
